content:
Nikhil Sharma: we need to settle tier naming before we lock console + docs copy. current: `fast / standard / cost-efficient`. question: do we want `fast` or `realtime` for the top tier?

Henry Cho: pls not `realtime` 😅 feels like it implies hard guarantees / “real-time systems” language.

Aditya Rao: +1. “realtime” also reads like streaming-only. fast tier is about tighter queue/wait budgets across streaming + non-streaming.

Alicia Perez: from UX POV, “realtime” sets expectation that it’s instantaneous. when it’s 700ms vs 1.2s users still feel “not realtime”.

Lauren Bishop: Dedicated customers will absolutely interpret “realtime” as “if it’s not realtime you’re breaching.” I’d rather avoid that word in contracts + QBRs.

Marissa Cole: also operationally… when we do overload behavior, fast tier is the first to shed / tighten admission. if we call it realtime, people will assume it never degrades.

Nikhil Sharma: what about `low-latency`? more explicit.

Henry Cho: low-latency is accurate but clunky. also doesn’t fit nicely in SDKs / headers.

Alicia Perez: in Console, “Low latency” looks ok, but in dropdowns it starts to feel technical. “Fast” reads better, but we need helper text.

Aditya Rao: + helper text can carry the nuance: “Fast = lowest tail latency targets; may reduce throughput under load.”

Sofia Ivanova: (looping in eng view) we’re tuning “fast” for tail protection, but it’s not “always fastest at p50” if the request mix is weird. calling it realtime is a foot-gun.

Nikhil Sharma: yeah, messaging pitfall is ppl think fast == always faster, regardless of workload.

Sean Gallagher: SRE POV: “realtime” increases incident pressure. if we page on p99 regressions for “realtime”, it’s gonna be ugly.

Elliot Price: docs angle: we can keep simple tier names, then define them precisely with SLO tables. “Fast” is fine as long as first paragraph says “lowest latency SLO tier (not a hard guarantee).”

Henry Cho: we should be careful with “not a hard guarantee” language too. it can read like “we don’t stand behind it.” maybe “targets and enforced protections, see SLOs.”

Lauren Bishop: +1. “target” is ok. in Dedicated we *do* have SLA constructs, but tier is a configuration. keep the tier description separate from SLA text.

Nikhil Sharma: ok. customer expectation risk: people might pick fast expecting “better UX” but then pay more / hit rate limits sooner.

Aditya Rao: right, need to call out tradeoff explicitly: fast == more conservative batching, lower throughput => higher $/token.

Alicia Perez: propose microcopy in UI:
- Fast: “Lowest latency (best for interactive/chat). Higher cost.”
- Standard: “Balanced latency + cost.”
- Cost-efficient: “Lowest cost (best for batch/offline). Higher latency.”

Henry Cho: careful w “higher cost” absolute. could be “typically higher cost” or “less cost-efficient”.

Alicia Perez: yep, “typically” works.

Sofia Ivanova: also “best for interactive/chat” is mostly true but not exclusively. streaming chat yes, but some non-streaming short prompts too. maybe “interactive workloads”.

Nikhil Sharma: what are the other name options ppl floated? I’ve heard `interactive` / `balanced` / `economy`.

Aditya Rao: “interactive” reads like a use case, not an SLO. also “interactive” doesn’t map cleanly to backend policy tier labels.

Lauren Bishop: “economy” is fine but we already used “cost-efficient” in the PRD drafts. economy also can sound like “lower quality” to some buyers.

Elliot Price: “economy” in docs historically triggers “is output worse?” questions. we need to keep quality separate from cost/latency.

Henry Cho: also avoid “premium” / “enterprise” style names. ppl will assume gating.

Marissa Cole: one more pitfall: if we call it “fast”, ppl might assume it disables safeguards like backpressure. we should say behavior under overload: fast will prioritize tail latency and may reject earlier.

Sean Gallagher: + please don’t promise “no queuing” or “no batching” for fast. it still batches, just tighter caps.

Nikhil Sharma: so far leaning: keep `fast` but define it carefully. any strong objections?

Lauren Bishop: no objection. just make sure Dedicated messaging includes: customer overrides > route policy > tier defaults. otherwise they’ll think “fast” overrides their cluster knobs.

Aditya Rao: we should add a FAQ line: “If I don’t pick a tier, what happens?” default to standard (balanced) unless route policy says otherwise.

Henry Cho: + another FAQ: “Does fast mean ‘real-time’?” answer: “Fast is our lowest-latency SLO tier; see published p95/p99 targets.”

Alicia Perez: can we avoid saying “not real-time”? it invites debate. maybe “Fast is designed for interactive latency targets.”

Elliot Price: agree. phrasing suggestion: “Fast is optimized for interactive applications with strict tail latency targets.”

Sofia Ivanova: and please add: “Fast may reduce throughput to protect p99.” This is the key behavior difference.

Nikhil Sharma: ok decision proposal:
1) Tier names remain `fast / standard / cost-efficient`
2) UI + docs: describe as “lowest latency / balanced / lowest cost”
3) Explicit tradeoffs: throughput + overload behavior
4) Avoid term “realtime” in customer-facing names

Henry Cho: :+1:

Lauren Bishop: :+1:

Alicia Perez: :+1: I’ll update console strings with “typically” qualifiers.

Elliot Price: I’ll incorporate into docs draft. will add a short “choosing a tier” section + FAQ on expectations.

Sean Gallagher: thank you. pls also route any “realtime” language to SRE review before it hits release notes.

Nikhil Sharma: done. I’ll reply in the PRD thread and tell runtime/docs we’re locking “fast” naming + the helper text direction.
